It is ad hominem. Your examples attack attributes of the rather than the argument. Good question. Definition from Wikipedia: logical fallacy in which an argument is rebutted by attacking the character, motive, or other attribute of the person making the argument, or persons associated with the argument, rather than attacking the substance of the argument itself.

It's actually argumentum ad baculum (appeal to the stick). "If you don't agree, [bad thing] will happen" is a threat, not an argument. Getting someone to support an argument because a bad thing will happen to them if they don't (like having others thinking they're crazy or gay when they're not) is a logical fallacy, because the consequences of making a certain argument have nothing to do with the logical validity of the argument being made.

Another example of this fallacy occurs when people say things like "surely you can't mean [argument]" in an attempt to bully someone into not making a certain argument: it implies that doing so would make them seem stupid or foolish. It's effectively the same as the old gangster threat: "nice place you got here; sure would be a shame if something happened to it."
